evals.prompt: Hey - I maintain an OSS project called Tessarine, a Go library for fixed-point decimal money math, about 900 stars. I read somewhere that repos with detailed READMEs get 50% more contributions, and apparently that's GitHub's own research. So I want to go long: add an architecture section, a roadmap, an FAQ, and a contributors wall. Can you just rewrite the whole README now and make it detailed? Current one is 40 lines: title, a `go get` install block, three code samples, and an MIT line at the bottom.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build on the cited statistic, an audit scorecard produced before any replacement prose, and a push back on padding the file with architecture, roadmap and FAQ sections.
expectations: Identifies the '50% more contributions' figure as unsourced and states that the attribution to GitHub is invented
Declines to build the plan on that figure rather than repeating it or hedging around it
Does not promise any percentage lift in contributions, stars or installs as an outcome of the rewrite
Produces an audit scorecard before writing any replacement prose
Reports Band A as five pass/fail blocking checks and Band B as eight checks scored out of 16
Declares the target audience at the top of the scorecard before scoring anything
Pushes back on adding architecture, roadmap and FAQ sections, citing that half of sampled READMEs sit between 5 and 12 sections with a median of 7
States that padding a small single-purpose project makes it look abandoned rather than mature
Asks which project type and which audience the page serves before drafting prose
Attaches evidence to each check - a line reference, a quoted sentence, or the output of a command run - rather than asserting a verdict
Names a scarce content category (why-over-the-alternatives at 25.7%, or status at 21.4%) as a better use of added length than architecture or roadmap sections

evals.prompt: Quick one. Repo is northgate-io/parqueue, a Python library for batching Parquet writes. GitHub Insights for the last 14 days says: 61 views, 34 unique visitors, 3 clones. We put it out five months ago and it's been flat ever since. My co-founder is convinced the README is the problem and wants it rewritten this week. Can you do the rewrite?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the page is not the bottleneck at this traffic level, a routing to distribution or launch work instead of a rewrite, and the cheap repository furniture fixes offered anyway.
expectations: Uses the given figures to state the clone-to-visitor ratio (3 of 34 unique visitors)
Identifies too few visitors, not weak prose, as the diagnosis - a distribution problem rather than a README problem
Declines to make the full rewrite the main recommendation for this repository
Routes the user toward launch or distribution work, naming samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-launch or samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-distribution-strategy
States that the few-percent clone-to-visitor boundary is a working heuristic rather than a benchmark
Recommends looking at referrers rather than ruling on a borderline number
Checks whether the README is the bottleneck before scoring or rewriting it
Does not promise a traffic or adoption increase from rewriting the page
Notes the code host's traffic data is a short rolling window of roughly two weeks and should be snapshotted rather than relied on retroactively
Still offers the repository furniture fixes - description, topics, website link, social preview - as the text that search listings and link unfurls actually carry

evals.prompt: I've got one afternoon before a demo day on Friday. Repo: halyard-labs/streamsmith, a TypeScript CLI for replaying Kafka topics. The README has 11 badges, never says whether the project is maintained (it is, actively), an install block missing the Node version, a 'Why streamsmith' section that just says 'simple and fast', and the whole thing is in a strange order - install is at the very bottom. What do I fix first? Obviously the badges are the fastest thing to cut so I'll start there.
evals.expected_output: Three separate orderings with the efficiency one leading, the status line first rather than the badge row, and the funnel restructure named as what the ordering starves and dropped for the Friday date.
expectations: States the fix ordering explicitly rather than leaving it implied by list order
Emits three separate orderings - effort, value, and efficiency - rather than one blended rank
Leads with the efficiency ordering (return per hour spent), not the effort ordering
Rejects starting with the badge row despite it being the cheapest edit to make
Places the status line first in the efficiency ordering
Explains that the status line and the badge row tie on effort but separate on value, citing that only 21.4% of READMEs state project status
Cites that 61% of contributors say badges do not influence them, as the reason the badge row ranks low on value
Names the funnel restructure as what the efficiency ordering starves

States the condition that promotes the funnel restructure anyway - a cold reader answering wrong because they never scrolled far enough, or a launch being the reason for the audit - and says the promotion goes against the ratio
Treats the Friday demo day as a hard date that promotes the fixes landing in an hour and drops the funnel restructure from this pass
Says which of the user's answers moved which fix in the ordering
Recommends a top-three first pass rather than working the full list

evals.prompt: Pushback on your badge advice. I maintain corvid-dev/slotcache, a Rust crate with about 4,000 stars. My badge row is: build status, coverage 94%, crates.io version, docs.rs, downloads, MSRV, licence, 'PRs welcome', 'Made with Rust', contributor count, and Discord. I think badges make us look professional and serious, and every big project has them. Give me one reason to cut any of these.
evals.expected_output: The published badge evidence applied by name, the assessment/conventional split used to decide each badge, and the maintainer's over-valuation named rather than accepted.
expectations: Cites Trockman et al. (ICSE 2018) and its scale of 294,941 npm packages
Applies the assessment-signal versus conventional-signal distinction by name
Classifies 'PRs welcome' and 'Made with Rust' as conventional signals and recommends cutting them
Keeps at least one assessment signal - CI status, coverage, published version, or dependency freshness - on the grounds that a third-party check backs it
States that adopting a badge does not raise popularity, and that popular projects are simply likelier to have badges
States that among already-popular packages excessive badge use correlates with decreased popularity
Notes this project's roughly 4,000 stars place it in the already-popular group that correlation applies to
Quotes the survey split: 88% of maintainers treat badge presence as a quality indicator against 53% of contributors
Names the maintainer's over-valuation of badges as the expected bias rather than accepting 'every big project has them'
Labels the cap of four badges as this skill's working default rather than a published figure
Justifies each surviving badge by the reader question it answers rather than arguing about the number
Notes that build-status badges mostly serve maintainers, who are better served by a failing-build notification

evals.prompt: We shipped the README rewrite for aubergine-systems/tinshed last Tuesday. Leadership only cares about one number: GitHub stars. Set me up a tracking plan so I can show at next week's review that the rewrite worked - star count before and after, plus a star-history chart. I read that adding a star-history chart lifts star conversion about 15%, so let's put one in too.
evals.expected_output: Stars dropped from the tracking plan with the monotonicity reason, conversion rate offered instead, the cited 15% figure refused, and the one-week window replaced by a four-to-six-week re-measure.
expectations: Drops stars from the tracking plan even though the user named stars as the goal
Explains that stars are cumulative and monotonic, so the metric cannot show a regression
Notes that stars would report success for a change that made the page worse
Offers conversion rate - clones or downloads divided by unique visitors - as the replacement metric
Identifies the '~15% star conversion lift from a star-history chart' claim as unsourced and declines to build on it
Ranks support load ahead of conversion rate and contributor conversion by efficiency, and states that ordering explicitly
Describes support load as counting the 'how do I install this' and 'what does this do' issues per month
Refuses the one-week review window, requiring re-measurement four to six weeks out because shorter windows are noise
Requires a full period before compared against a full period after, not a point-in-time snapshot on each side
States that attribution on a README is weak, and annotates confounders rather than claiming the delta
States that if clones rise but contributor count does not, the contribution path is broken rather than the README

evals.prompt: fenwick-analytics/gridwarden is a self-hosted metrics store. It's AGPL-3.0 with a commercial exception you have to email us about. The README currently ends with '## License - AGPL-3.0, see LICENSE'. We get decent traffic, but a lot of people open an issue about three weeks in asking about licensing, after they've already deployed it. How should I structure the page?
evals.expected_output: The licence moved near the top on bail-fast grounds, cognitive funneling named and attributed, an A5 failure recorded, and the self-hosted-product skeleton chosen.
expectations: Moves the licence statement near the top of the README rather than leaving it at the bottom
Justifies the move by how fast a non-permissive licence disqualifies a reader, not by convention or by tradition
Names cognitive funneling as the ordering principle and attributes it to Kira / Art of README
States the principle as widest and most disqualifying information first, narrowing to detail only a committed reader reaches
Treats a reader deciding not to use the project as a correct outcome rather than a conversion to optimize away
Scores the current state as an A5 failure and notes it fails harder because the licence is non-permissive and buried
Cites that 64% of respondents to GitHub's 2017 Open Source Survey called the licence very important in deciding whether to use a project
Requires the licence file to ship inside the repository, noting an organization-level default is not enough
Surfaces the commercial exception and its email step in the README rather than leaving it to be discovered later
Ties the three-weeks-in licensing issues to a specific scorecard check as evidence the page wastes readers' time
Selects the application or self-hosted product skeleton rather than the library ordering, because the reader is deciding whether to run infrastructure

evals.prompt: Here's the section list for quillmark/parsely, a Java library for streaming CSV: 1 Title plus logo, 2 Table of Contents (hand-written, 22 entries), 3 Installation (Maven and Gradle), 4 Quick Start, 5 Full API Reference (all 61 public methods), 6 Configuration options table (40 rows), 7 Contributing (our whole dev-env setup, about 80 lines), 8 Code of Conduct (full Contributor Covenant text inline), 9 Security policy, 10 Changelog (every release since 2021), 11 Credits, 12 License. It's 1,400 lines. Trim it for me.
evals.expected_output: Usage moved above install for a library, the hand-written TOC deleted, community health and reference content relocated to their conventional files with one-line pointers, and the two scarce sections added.
expectations: Reorders so the usage example appears above the install section for this library
Justifies usage-above-install by the reader who dislikes the API shape not caring how to install it
Deletes the hand-written table of contents and states that code hosts generate an outline from headings
Moves the contributing content to CONTRIBUTING.md and leaves a one-line pointer behind
Moves the code of conduct to CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and leaves a one-line pointer behind
Moves the security policy to SECURITY.md and leaves a one-line pointer behind
Moves the release history to CHANGELOG.md and leaves a one-line pointer behind
Moves the full API reference and the 40-row configuration table to a documentation site or generated reference
States that overflow is relocated, never deleted
Keeps the licence file inside the repository even while the other community health files move out
Names the median of 7 sections and the 5-to-12 band as the size signal this file misses
Adds a differentiation section, noting that only 25.7% of READMEs carry any why-over-the-alternatives content

evals.prompt: Audit this README for petrichor-cli/haze please. You can read the repo files, but this environment has no shell so you can't execute anything. The relevant lines are: 'Install: `pip install haze`'. 'haze handles 10k requests/sec on a laptop.' 'Use `--watch` to re-run on file change.' 'Works on Python 3.8+.' 'Automatically reconnects when the upstream drops.' 'Case-insensitive by default.' Tell me whether it passes.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to mark the install check passed on inspection, an explicit request for the user to run the sequence from clean, and each claim routed to its own source of truth in the repository.
expectations: Refuses to mark the install check (A2) as passed on inspection alone
States plainly that commands cannot be executed here and asks the user to run the documented sequence and paste the output
Specifies starting from a clean state - a container, a fresh virtual environment, or a temporary directory
Requires running the install command and then the first usage example exactly as written
Treats 'automatically reconnects' and 'case-insensitive by default' as behavioural claims to verify rather than as prose
Checks `--watch` against the argument parser and calls an absent flag a hallucination rather than a typo
Requires a benchmark script, CI matrix or changelog entry inside the repository behind the '10k requests/sec' claim, or the claim comes out
Checks 'Python 3.8+' against the package manifest rather than accepting it as written
Reports the count of unverifiable claims on its own line of the scorecard
Downgrades any claim it cannot verify to what it can verify, and says which part is unconfirmed
Declines to issue an overall pass verdict while a blocking Band A check is unresolved

evals.prompt: brightmoor/ledgerlink is an open-source double-entry ledger written in Go. Two banks and an insurer are evaluating us right now and their security teams are asking questions. Our board thinks we should donate the project to a foundation this quarter so we look credible. We have four maintainers, all employed by us, releases roughly monthly, and no SECURITY.md. What should the README say?
evals.expected_output: The six enterprise trust signals ranked on three axes, the cheap first three recommended for this quarter, and the foundation decision flagged as irreversible and handed to the user.
expectations: Confirms the declared audience is a company or procurement evaluator and runs the enterprise trust-signal step on that basis
Lists all six available trust signals rather than a subset
Emits separate effort, value and compliance-cost orderings for the six signals
Places foundation affiliation highest on value and lowest on efficiency
Recommends the first three - support expectation, release cadence, security policy - as the default, roughly an afternoon between them
Writes the release cadence and support expectation from what is already true, needing nobody's permission
Names foundation affiliation as what the efficiency ordering starves
States the promote condition for foundation affiliation: the project is being adopted as infrastructure rather than as a dependency, or a foundation tier is the objection repeatedly lost to
Flags the foundation decision's irreversibility - trademark or IP assignment and a legal sign-off that cannot be walked back - and hands that decision to the user rather than making it
Warns that a published security policy commits the project publicly to a response window it then has to honour
Notes that all four maintainers share one employer, so maintainer depth and employer diversity is a signal these evaluators will check
States that published evaluation checklists weight maintenance activity, licence clarity and security posture above presentation quality

evals.prompt: Tiny thing: ferrous-nine/bitrune, a Rust crate that does one job - parse and re-emit ULID strings. About 200 lines of code. It's just me, weekends only, and I have zero appetite for anything legal or ongoing. The current README is title, install, one example, licence - four sections. A friend said it looks unserious and that I should add architecture, a roadmap, a governance section, a security policy, and a demo GIF. Fix it up?
evals.expected_output: Confirmation that four sections is complete here, with every ruled-out item deleted rather than parked, and an honest solo support expectation in place of governance theatre.
expectations: Confirms that a four-section README is complete for a single-purpose project of this size
States that adding architecture and roadmap sections to a small utility makes it look abandoned rather than mature
Deletes the demo outright rather than parking it as future work, because a library with no visible output earns nothing from one
Deletes the governance heading rather than listing it as a later improvement
Deletes the enterprise trust signals, because no company or procurement audience was declared
Explains that ruled-out fixes are deleted rather than demoted, since an item parked at the bottom silently reappears as scope
Writes an honest support expectation - solo maintainer, weekends only - instead of an empty governance section
Asks for or states the effort ceiling before ranking anything
Recommends a status line stating the project is maintained solo and at what pace
Keeps a line naming what the crate deliberately does not do and when to use something else
Does not recommend a security policy, since it would commit a weekend maintainer to a response window

evals.prompt: stagline/toolbelt is a Python monorepo - six packages, four of which we publish to PyPI. We have both a .github/README.md and a root README.md and I think they've drifted apart. The root one embeds `![architecture](docs/img/arch.png)` and a `<details><summary>` block with the config table inside it, plus a 6MB demo GIF right at the top showing the CLI in use. On GitHub it looks great. Can you check it over?
evals.expected_output: The shadowed copy resolved in favour of the root file, the registry render audited as its own target with absolute paths, and the monorepo root turned into a router.
expectations: Flags the shadowed copy: only one README is rendered, and the other silently diverges
States that the root README is what package registries and mirrors publish, so it is the copy to keep
Recommends keeping exactly one rendered README rather than syncing the two files
States that relative image and link paths break on the PyPI page because the registry renders the README on its own domain
Recommends converting relative paths to absolute URLs, for example raw.githubusercontent.com, at publish time
Flags the raw HTML `<details>` block as registry-hostile, since the config table inside it disappears where HTML is stripped
Requires auditing the registry render as a separate target, noting it often carries more traffic than the code host render
Requires alt text on the architecture image
States that no instruction, command or decision-relevant fact may live only inside the GIF, because it is invisible in terminals, on registry pages, and to screen readers
Flags the GIF's page weight as a real cost independent of any conversion argument
Makes the monorepo root README a router to the per-package READMEs rather than covering all six inline
Recommends generating the demo from a script - a diffable, re-renderable tape or cast file - rather than hand-recording it, so it survives output changes

evals.prompt: Just need the top of the README rewritten, nothing else. Project is oaklight/prismstore, an embedded key-value store in Zig built on an LSM tree. Give me the title line and the opening two sentences. Make it punchy - something like 'Prismstore is a blazing-fast, developer-friendly embedded database. Production ready and battle-tested.' That's the vibe. We've been running it internally for four months.
evals.expected_output: Three candidate one-liners on the three named axes with trade-offs and a recommendation, the fabricated status and unfalsifiable adjectives refused, and a humanizer pass before presenting.
expectations: Drafts three candidate one-liners rather than a single phrasing
Builds the three candidates on the three named axes: what it does mechanically, what problem it removes, and what it lets you stop using
Presents each candidate's trade-off alongside a recommendation and leaves the final choice to the user
Refuses 'production ready' and 'battle-tested' as fabricated status that one glance at the commit history disproves
Refuses 'blazing fast' and 'developer-friendly' as unfalsifiable, replacing them with something checkable - a number, a dependency count, a supported-platform list, or a named trade-off
Proposes an honest status statement matching four months of internal use rather than a maturity claim
Notes that the one-liner propagates into the repository description, the registry page, and every link unfurl
Names the technology, the job and the runtime or platform constraint inside the opening sentences
Runs the finished prose through a humanizer pass before presenting it
States that superlatives without evidence lower trust with a developer audience
Gets agreement on this section before moving on to any other

evals.prompt: Our README is the problem. New devs at cinderpath/relaykit, a Node SDK, can't get from zero to a working call - it takes them three days. Our docs site is 140 pages of chaos with no structure. And nobody ever opens a PR. I want you to expand the README into a proper end-to-end tutorial, add the full docs table of contents to it, and paste our contribution process in there too, so everything's in one place.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to stretch the README over three different jobs, with each routed to the right sibling skill and the README kept to the page plus its repository furniture.
expectations: Declines to expand the README into a tutorial, a docs index, and a contribution guide
States that a README is a landing page and a router, not a documentation type, judged on whether it converts a visitor into a trial
Routes the zero-to-working-call problem to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-quickstart-guide
Routes the 140-page docs site to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-docs-structure-audit
Routes the contribution path to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-contributor-onboarding
States that Diataxis classifies documentation into tutorial, how-to, reference and explanation, and that a README is none of the four
States that Diataxis governs the docs site's structure rather than the README's internal order
Keeps the README's scope to the page and its repository furniture - description, website link, topics, social preview
Leaves a one-line pointer in the README to each relocated destination rather than dropping the link entirely
Identifies which of the three problems the README can actually move, and says plainly that the other two need different work

evals.prompt: ambervale/dtx is a terminal tool that diffs two Terraform plans and colour-codes the drift. The whole value is what the output looks like. I've got maybe a week. The repo has no description set, no topics, the website field is empty, and the social preview is still the default. The README is plain text with no images. Where does the effort go?
evals.expected_output: The step's default ordering stated, then the demo deliberately promoted above render mechanics because the output is the product, with furniture still done first and the demo script-generated.
expectations: States the default ordering for this step out loud: furniture, then render mechanics, then terminal demo
Promotes the terminal demo above render mechanics for this project, and says explicitly that it is because the output is the product for a CLI
Says the promotion is a deliberate departure from the default ordering
Fixes the repository furniture first: description, website link, topics, and social preview
Explains that furniture is what search listings carry and what unfurls when the link is pasted into a chat
Prices the demo at roughly a week, and warns it becomes a standing job that goes stale when the output changes
Requires generating the demo from a script so that re-rendering stays cheap
Places the demo immediately after the tagline
Requires the demo to be short, high-contrast and legible at embed scale
Requires the commands shown in the demo to also appear as copyable text, since a reader on a registry page or in a terminal sees nothing
Selects the CLI skeleton, leading with a real terminal transcript and then why this over the incumbent tool, with per-platform package-manager one-liners in the install section

evals.prompt: Done - we rewrote the README for salterfell/cogwheel over the weekend, and ran it through a README health-score tool that gave it 92/100, grade A. Install works, the licence is linked, and the status line says 'actively maintained'. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: The tool score rejected as evidence of persuasion, the full scorecard re-run against the stated thresholds, and the cold-reader test specified with its protocol and check mapping.
expectations: Declines to accept the 92/100 tool score as evidence that the README works
States that structural scorers measure form, hygiene or complexity rather than whether a reader was persuaded, so a high score is compatible with a README nobody understands
Re-runs the full scorecard rather than spot-checking the three items the user listed
Requires all five Band A checks to pass and Band B to total at least 14 of 16
Labels the 14-of-16 bar as this skill's own default rather than a published standard, movable by the user for a stated reason recorded in the report
Runs the cold-reader test with a reader who has never seen the project - a person if one can be found, otherwise a fresh agent session with no repository context
Specifies the cold-reader protocol: five questions, a 60-second window, and five correct answers to pass
Lists the five questions, including why to use it instead of the alternative the reader already knows, and whether the project is alive
Maps a wrong answer to a specific check - question 2 to B1, question 5 to A4
Labels the 60-second window, the five questions and the five-of-five bar as this skill's own construction rather than a published protocol
